questions.q: Which of the following biochemical processes is fundamentally accelerated in diabetic patients and contributes to microangiopathic complications including retinopathy and nephropathy?
opts: Enzymatic degradation of elastic fibers by increased metalloproteinase activity
Non-enzymatic glycosylation of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids forming advanced glycation end products
Increased production of androgens by ovarian tissue in response to hyperglycemia
Enhanced chemotaxis and bactericidal activity of neutrophils in hyperglycemic states
questions.exp: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) form through non-enzymatic glycosylation when glucose and fructose bind to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. This process is greatly accelerated in diabetes and AGE accumulation is responsible for dermatological manifestations and microangiopathic complications like retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. Glycated collagen resists degradation and accumulates in the dermis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with cervical cancer is found to have high-risk HPV infection. Which viral proteins are primarily responsible for the malignant transformation observed in this case?
opts: L1 and L2 capsid proteins that promote viral assembly
E6 and E7 proteins that inactivate p53 and retinoblastoma protein
E1 and E2 proteins involved in viral DNA replication
Late proteins that facilitate viral shedding from epithelial cells
questions.exp: The oncogenic potential of high-risk HPV types is directly linked to E6 and E7 proteins. E6 inactivates p53 (a critical tumor suppressor), while E7 inhibits retinoblastoma protein (pRb), disrupting cell cycle control and leading to cellular immortalization and malignant transformation. The L1/L2 proteins are structural capsid proteins used in vaccines, not oncogenic factors.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient with HIV infection (CD4 count 120 cells/μL) undergoes tuberculin skin testing as part of TB screening. After intradermal injection of 5 TU PPD into the volar forearm, the test is read at 72 hours and shows 3 mm of induration. What is the correct interpretation of this result?
opts: Negative test; patient does not have TB infection
Positive test; indicates TB infection in this high-risk group
Indeterminate; requires repeat testing in 2 weeks
False negative due to anergy; cannot exclude active TB
questions.exp: In severely immunosuppressed patients (HIV with CD4 <200), an induration of ≥5 mm is considered positive. This patient's 3 mm induration falls below this threshold, but HIV/AIDS is a major cause of anergy leading to false negatives. Active TB cannot be excluded despite the negative TST result, and further investigation is warranted.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture an HIV patient in the castle dungeon so immunosuppressed their WALLS CRUMBLE (anergy)—the tuberculin invader sneaks past because the immune guards are dead. A negative TST in AIDS is a TRAP, not a pass.

questions.q: A 45-year-old kidney transplant recipient on long-term calcineurin inhibitors develops multiple squamous cell carcinomas. Compared to immunocompetent individuals, which statement about SCC risk and phenotype in this patient is most accurate?
opts: SCC risk is increased 2–5 fold, and the BCC-to-SCC ratio remains 4:1 as in the general population
SCC risk is increased 65–250 fold, the normal 4:1 BCC-to-SCC ratio is reversed to 1:4, and SCCs exhibit more aggressive behavior
SCC risk is increased due to HPV-16/HPV-18 infection exclusively, with a protective effect against metastasis
SCC risk is decreased because calcineurin inhibitors provide a paradoxical anti-tumorigenic effect on keratinocytes
questions.exp: Solid organ transplant recipients face a dramatic 65–250-fold increased SCC risk, with the typical BCC-to-SCC ratio of 4:1 reversed to 1:4. These immunosuppressed patients' SCCs are notably more aggressive, exhibiting higher metastatic rates and disease-specific mortality compared to immunocompetent individuals. This represents a qualitative and quantitative shift in skin cancer epidemiology in this high-risk population.
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a TRANSPLANT PATIENT at a SEESAW in the castle courtyard — the BCC side (4) shoots UP into the sky while the SCC side (1) CRASHES down. Now flip it UPSIDE DOWN (1:4) and watch SCCs become ANGRY MONSTERS (aggressive, metastatic) on the immunosuppressed playground.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with pemphigus vulgaris is being started on oral prednisolone and a purine synthesis inhibitor for corticosteroid-sparing effect. Between azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), which agent would be preferentially chosen if the patient has baseline creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL indicating mild renal impairment?
opts: Mycophenolate mofetil, because it has faster onset of action in all patient populations
Azathioprine, because it is generally preferred in patients with renal impairment
Mycophenolate mofetil, because it does not require TPMT screening prior to initiation
Azathioprine, because it is more potent than MMF in autoimmune blistering diseases
questions.exp: Azathioprine is generally preferred in patients with renal impairment compared to mycophenolate mofetil. However, azathioprine requires mandatory pre-treatment screening of thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) to prevent life-threatening myelosuppression, whereas MMF demonstrates faster treatment responses when added to corticosteroids.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with suspected tinea capitis. Wood's lamp examination reveals a brilliant blue-green fluorescence of the entire hair shaft. Which organism is most likely responsible for this infection?
opts: Trichophyton tonsurans
Microsporum canis
Trichophyton violaceum
Microsporum gypseum
questions.exp: Microsporum canis and Microsporum audouinii produce a characteristic brilliant blue-green fluorescence of the entire hair shaft under Wood's lamp examination. The fluorescence is caused by a fungal metabolite called pteridine. In contrast, most Trichophyton species (T. tonsurans, T. violaceum) do not fluoresce, and M. gypseum produces only a dull-yellow fluorescence.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture MICROSPORUM dressed in BRILLIANT BLUE-GREEN ballgown dancing through the castle hair ballroom—she's the ONLY one shining like a DISCO BALL at the royal tinea party.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with velvety hyperpigmented plaques on his neck, axillae, and groin. Histopathologically, the lesion shows hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis with minimal acanthosis. Which pathogenic mechanism is primarily responsible for this clinical presentation?
opts: Non-enzymatic glycosylation of collagen leading to reduced skin elasticity
Hyperinsulinemia stimulating IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts
Impaired wound healing secondary to macroangiopathic complications
Decreased chemotaxis and phagocytosis of white blood cells
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans in diabetes is mediated by hyperinsulinemia acting on insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) receptors in keratinocytes and fibroblasts, stimulating epidermal proliferation manifesting as hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis. The histopathology showing minimal acanthosis despite the clinical appearance rules out the other mechanisms listed. AGEs affect collagen structure but are not the primary driver of acanthosis nigricans pathogenesis.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with a rapidly enlarging, bright red pedunculated papule on his finger that bleeds easily. Histopathology shows lobular proliferations of small capillaries within a fibromyxoid stroma bounded by an epithelial collarette. According to ISSVA classification, what is the correct categorization of this lesion?
opts: Vascular malformation—capillary type
Benign vascular tumour
Congenital vascular anomaly requiring early intervention
Granulomatous inflammatory disorder
questions.exp: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) is classified by ISSVA strictly under 'Benign Vascular Tumours,' explicitly separating it from vascular malformations. It is an acquired, benign vascular proliferation despite its misleading historical name.

questions.q: A newborn at 6 hours of life is noted to be encased in a shiny, taut, parchment-like membrane that subsequently sheds over the first few days. After membrane shedding, generalized erythroderma with fine, feathery scales develops. Associated findings include ectropion, eclabium, and cicatricial alopecia. Which inheritance pattern and primary genetic defect characterize this condition?
opts: Autosomal dominant; KRT1/KRT10 mutations affecting keratin structure
Autosomal recessive; ARCI-spectrum genes affecting stratum corneum lipid processing
Autosomal dominant; SPINK5 mutations causing unregulated desquamation
Autosomal recessive; TGM1 mutations alone without other lipid defects
questions.exp: Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (non-bullous CIIE) presents with a collodion membrane at birth (90% of cases) and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern with defects in the ARCI spectrum including ALOX12B, ALOXE3, NIPAL4, PNPLA1, CERS3, and TGM1 genes—all involved in stratum corneum lipid processing and transport. The collodion membrane shedding followed by persistent erythroderma and associated ectodermal features is pathognomonic.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: A NEWBORN WRAPPED in a SHINY PARCHMENT CLOAK (collodion membrane) peels it away to reveal a LIPID-DEFICIENT KINGDOM (ARCI spectrum—ALOX, NIPAL4, PNPLA1) where TEARS stream from DROOPING EYES (ectropion) and HAIR FAILS to grow (cicatricial alopecia).

questions.q: Why is the historical term 'pyogenic granuloma' considered a double misnomer?
opts: It is infected by pyogenic bacteria and contains true granulomatous inflammation
It is neither pyogenic in origin nor a true granuloma histologically
It produces purulent exudate but lacks epithelioid cells
It is pyogenic but lacks the capillary proliferation seen on microscopy
questions.exp: The lesion is devoid of pyogenic (bacterial) origin and produces no true purulent exudate, and it completely lacks granulomatous histological architecture (multinucleated giant cells and epithelioid histiocytes). Instead, it is a reactive vascular hyperplasia mimicking exuberantly proliferating granulation tissue.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the epidemiology and nomenclature of erythema toxicum neonatorum is correct?
opts: The condition typically appears within the first 6–12 hours after birth in preterm infants
The name 'erythema toxicum' accurately reflects an infectious and toxic process in the neonatal period
ETN is rare in premature infants and occurs most commonly in full-term newborns over 2500 g
The eruption was first described by Leiner and named 'toxic erythema' because maternal toxins trigger the immune response
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum is fundamentally a disease of healthy, full-term infants weighing >2500 g; it is rare in preterm or low-birth-weight neonates. The name is a misnomer—there is no toxic component, infectious agent, or systemic toxicity. The condition was first described by Nettlinger and the eponym introduced by Leiner in 1912, but represents a benign innate-immune response to commensal microbes.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions

questions.q: A 2-year-old male with anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia presents with recurrent severe bacterial infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, and defective NK cell cytotoxicity. Which genetic mutation best explains the addition of immunodeficiency to his phenotype?
opts: NEMO (IKBKG) gene mutation encoding NF-κB essential modulator
EDA gene mutation encoding ectodysplasin A
EDAR gene mutation encoding ectodysplasin A receptor
COL17A1 gene mutation encoding type XVII collagen
questions.exp: Anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency (EDA-ID) is caused by NEMO/IKBKG mutations, resulting in defective NF-κB signaling that impairs both ectodermal development and immune cell function. This X-linked recessive condition is extremely rare (~1 in 250,000 male births) and combines classic ED features with severe antibody and NK cell defects.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine the NEMO GOLDFISH (NEMO gene) TRAPPED in an NF-κB CASTLE DUNGEON—without him, both the SWEAT GUARDS (anhidrosis) AND the IMMUNE KNIGHTS (antibodies, NK cells) abandon their posts, leaving the kingdom defenseless against BACTERIAL INVADERS storming through the gates.

questions.q: A 28-year-old healthcare worker with no known TB exposure history presents with an induration of 12 mm on tuberculin skin testing read at 48 hours. According to risk stratification thresholds, this result should be interpreted as:
opts: Positive; ≥10 mm threshold applies to healthcare workers as a high-risk group
Negative; requires ≥15 mm for positivity in this low-risk category
Indeterminate; healthcare workers require a separate threshold of 8 mm
Positive only if accompanied by a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay
questions.exp: Healthcare workers are classified as high-risk individuals, for whom a TST induration of ≥10 mm is considered positive. This patient's 12 mm induration meets the high-risk threshold and indicates TB infection status. The ≥15 mm threshold applies only to low-risk individuals with no known risk factors.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A HEALTHCARE HERO guards the castle at the ≥10mm BARRIER—one notch lower than the peasant's ≥15mm wall because they face constant TB danger.

questions.q: A 2-day-old full-term male infant presents with scattered 1–3 mm firm papules topped by white pustules on the cheeks, forehead, and trunk, surrounded by blotchy erythema. Pustule smear shows predominantly eosinophils with occasional neutrophils; culture is sterile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Neonatal herpes simplex infection
Erythema toxicum neonatorum
Infantile acropustulosis
Transient neonatal pustular melanosis
questions.exp: The clinical presentation—transient papulopustules appearing 24–48 hours after birth with characteristic 'flea-bitten' appearance (central pustule surrounded by erythematous halo), sterile pustule culture, and smear predominance of eosinophils—is pathognomonic for erythema toxicum neonatorum. ETN affects 48–72% of healthy full-term newborns and is benign and self-limiting.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions

questions.q: A 68-year-old fair-skinned male with a 40-year history of outdoor construction work presents with a lesion on his bald scalp. Histopathology confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following best explains why SCC, rather than BCC, is the predominant skin cancer type in this patient?
opts: SCC is driven by intermittent, intense sun exposure with blistering sunburns, while BCC arises from chronic cumulative exposure
SCC is primarily associated with chronic, cumulative lifetime UV exposure, in contrast to melanoma's association with intermittent intense exposure
SCC preferentially develops in individuals with Fitzpatrick phototype III-IV skin, whereas this patient's fair skin predisposes to BCC
SCC has a significantly lower metastatic potential than BCC, making it more likely to develop in outdoor workers
questions.exp: Cutaneous SCC is distinctly driven by chronic, cumulative lifetime UV exposure, distinguishing it from melanoma which correlates with intermittent, intense blistering sunburns. The patient's occupational sun exposure history directly supports SCC pathogenesis. Fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick I-II) who burn easily are indeed at highest risk, and SCC arises on chronically sun-exposed sites like the scalp.
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CONSTRUCTION WORKER slowly toasting like BREAD in an OVEN for decades (chronic cumulative UV) — his scalp turns golden, then CRISPY with SCC. Melanoma workers get FLASH-BURNED once; SCC workers get SLOW-ROASTED forever.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with fine, white-gray flaky scales predominantly on his elbows and knees. His palms show a hyperlinear pattern, and he has a history of asthma. The flexural areas and diaper region are notably spared. Which genetic mutation is responsible for this presentation?
opts: Loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene encoding filaggrin
Deletion of the STS gene on chromosome Xp22.3
Mutation in ABCA12 causing lipid transport defects
Gap junction protein mutation in GJB1
questions.exp:
Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the FLG gene on chromosome 1q21, which encodes filaggrin—a protein critical for keratin aggregation in the stratum granulosum and natural moisturizing factor production. The clinical presentation of fine scales on extensor surfaces, hyperlinear palms, and flexural sparing is pathognomonic for IV. Histology shows a characteristic diminished or absent stratum granulosum.
🏰 Palace: Imagine FILAGGRIN as a FACTORY WORKER gluing down BRICKS (keratin) in the STRATUM GRANULOSUM castle—when the factory closes (FLG mutation), the bricks scatter as fine white FLAKES on the ELBOWS, but the HIDDEN FLEXURAL DUNGEONS stay clean because the worker never worked there.

questions.q: A 28-year-old adult presents with symmetric, itchy edema and erythema of the hands and feet with a sharply demarcated border at the wrists and ankles. Petechiae and purpuric papules are noted on the dorsal fingers. Histopathology reveals viral structural proteins within dermal blood vessel walls. Which parvovirus-associated syndrome is this patient most likely experiencing?
opts: Classic erythema infectiosum with atypical presentation
Papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS)
Infectious erythema multiforme
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
questions.exp: Papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) is a distinct acral variant of parvovirus B19 characterized by sharply demarcated symmetric erythema and purpura of the distal hands and feet, with histologic detection of viral proteins in dermal blood vessel walls. Unlike classic fifth disease in school-aged children, PPGSS predominantly affects young adults.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with anhidrosis, saddle facies, sparse fuzzy hair, and peg-shaped conical teeth. His mother is mildly affected with localized anhidrosis and missing lower incisors. What is the most likely genetic inheritance pattern and molecular basis of this disorder?
opts: X-linked recessive due to EDA gene mutation encoding ectodysplasin A
Autosomal dominant due to EDAR receptor mutation
Autosomal recessive due to EDARADD adaptor protein mutation
X-linked dominant with male lethality
questions.exp: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome) is most commonly X-linked recessive due to EDA gene mutations, affecting >90% of severely affected males while carrier females show mild, patchy features via X-inactivation (lyonization). The mother's mild presentation confirms her carrier status with asymmetric X-inactivation.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a MALE PRINCE (>90% males affected) sitting in the CASTLE NURSERY (anhidrotic ED), his mother HALF-HIDDEN behind X-CHROMOSOME CURTAINS (carrier with patchy features), both with CONICAL CROWNS on their heads (peg teeth) and SADDLE-SHAPED NOSES—the EDA GENE SCEPTER controls it all from the X-THRONE.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with a bright red, confluent macular erythema strictly limited to the cheeks with sparing of the nasal bridge and circumoral regions. The mother reports a mild prodrome of low-grade fever and headache 3 days prior. What is the most likely diagnosis and the current infectious status of the patient?
opts: Erythema infectiosum (Fifth Disease); patient is still infectious
Erythema infectiosum (Fifth Disease); patient is no longer infectious
Measles; patient remains highly infectious
Scarlet fever; patient requires immediate antibiotic therapy
questions.exp: The classic 'slapped cheek' appearance in a school-aged child following a mild prodrome is pathognomonic for erythema infectiosum caused by Human Parvovirus B19. A crucial clinical pearl is that the patient becomes non-infectious once the cutaneous rash appears, which occurs after the initial viremia and systemic symptoms.

questions.q: During Wood's lamp examination of a patient with suspected pityriasis versicolor, the clinician observes a pale yellowish-white fluorescence of the scales. What is the primary mechanism underlying this fluorescence?
opts: Production of porphyrins by Malassezia furfur
Deposition of lipid metabolites on the stratum corneum
Fluorescence caused by pteridine produced by Malassezia furfur
Activation of melanin by long-wave ultraviolet radiation
questions.exp: Only Malassezia furfur has been definitively linked to fluorescence in pityriasis versicolor, and the mechanism involves production of a fungal metabolite called pteridine (the same metabolite responsible for Microsporum fluorescence in tinea capitis). This fluorescence appears as pale yellowish-white or yellow coloration under Wood's lamp examination.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture MALASSEZIA sitting in the castle library writing a PTERIDINE YELLOW-GREEN love letter—she's the ONLY mailbox producing PALE YELLOW GLOW at the versicolor ball.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with severe plaque psoriasis affecting 60% of his body surface area is being considered for systemic therapy. Which of the following best describes the fundamental principle that should guide the decision to initiate systemic therapy in this patient?
opts: The risk of the systemic drug regimen must never exceed the innate risk and morbidity of the underlying disease
Systemic therapy should only be used if topical therapies have been applied for at least 12 months without improvement
All patients with >50% BSA involvement should automatically receive combination systemic and biologic therapy
Systemic therapy is contraindicated unless the patient has documented organ involvement secondary to psoriasis
questions.exp: The risk-risk assessment principle mandates that the clinician ensures the risk of the planned systemic drug regimen never exceeds the innate risk and morbidity of the underlying disease being treated. This is the foundational philosophy governing all systemic prescribing in dermatology, emphasizing judicious and evidence-based decision-making rather than automatic escalation.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with a painful lesion on his palm that has gradually enlarged over 6 months. On examination, a keratotic papule is noted. Which HPV type is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: HPV-6
HPV-1
HPV-16
HPV-31
questions.exp: HPV-1 is site-specific and typically replicates in the heavily keratinized skin of palms and soles, making it the most likely causative agent for a wart on the palm. This contrasts with HPV-16, which prefers genital areas, and HPV-6, which is associated with genital warts. HPV-31 is a high-risk oncogenic type found in anogenital regions.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with generalized erythroderma, superficial blistering, and erosions. On examination, you note corrugated, cobblestone-like hyperkeratosis predominantly in the flexures and a pungent odor. Histopathology reveals epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with vacuolar degeneration of the suprabasal layers and dense keratin intermediate filament clumps. Which genetic defect is most likely responsible?
opts: Mutations in KRT1 and KRT10 genes
Mutations in ALOXE3 and ALOX12B genes
Mutations in SPINK5 gene
Mutations in NIPAL4 (ichthyin) gene
questions.exp: Epidermolytic ichthyosis (bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma) is caused by mutations in KRT1 and KRT10 genes encoding keratin intermediate filaments in the suprabasal epidermis, resulting in the pathognomonic finding of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. The autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and spontaneous mutation rate of 50% make new mutations common in neonatal presentations.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture a KNIGHT (KRT1/KRT10) whose ARMOR (keratin filaments) SHATTERS into epidermolytic BLISTERS in the CASTLE'S UPPER TOWERS (suprabasal layers), leaving behind COBBLESTONE ruins and a FOUL SMELL in the DUNGEON.

questions.q: A 2-week-old male infant is noted to have large, thick, dark-brown polygonal scales that involve the neck, preauricular region, and flexures, giving a 'dirty neck' appearance. Maternal serum cholesterol sulfate is markedly elevated. Which of the following clinical features would you NOT expect to find in this condition?
opts: Hyperlinear palms and soles
Comma-shaped corneal opacities in adulthood
Increased risk of cryptorchidism
Flexural involvement and lateral facial scaling
questions.exp:
Recessive X-linked ichthyosis (RXLI) is caused by steroid sulfatase deficiency due to STS gene deletion on Xp22.3, leading to cholesterol sulfate accumulation. Unlike ichthyosis vulgaris, RXLI completely spares the palms and soles (no hyperlinear pattern) and characteristically involves flexures and the preauricular region. Systemic features include comma-shaped corneal opacities (50% of males) and a 20-fold increased cryptorchidism risk.
🏰 Palace: Picture a DIRTY NECK KING (RXLI) sitting backwards on his THRONE—his FLEXURES are FILTHY with dark scales, but his PALMS are PRISTINE and CLEAN (no hyperlinearity), and his EYES have COMMA TAILS (corneal opacities) watching from the castle windows.
